newsitem.title: CANADA: Nickel market ignores Inco lockout for now.
newsitem.headline: Nickel market ignores Inco lockout for now.

text.p: The world nickel market has turned a blind eye to a week-long labor dispute that has halted production at Inco Ltd's Manitoba facility.
But if the dispute drags on long enough, nickel prices will start to rise, analysts and industry official said.
Inco shut down the plant a week ago, locking out almost 1,400 members of the United Steelworkers after they voted to reject the company's final contract offer.
The Thompson facility produces about 100 million pounds of nickel a year, or about 20 percent of Inco's total output.
The labor dispute has so far had little impact on nickel prices, despite a delicate balance in world supply and demand that has kept the commodity price in check for months.
"Nickel is just holding in there," Patricia Mohr, economist for Bank of Nova Scotia, said in an interview.
"The base metal markets are very quiet. I think they're waiting for industrial demand to pick up."
A surplus of stainless steel, which absorbs about two-thirds of the world nickel supply, has kept a rise in the nickel price at bay, she said.
But the nickel price will eventually react, she added.
The cash price for nickel on the London Metal Exchange has fallen steadily since the lockout began.

With no production from Inco's Thompson facility, and output cut by a third at Inco's Indonesia facility because of a broken furnace, steady nickel demand will eventually start eating into inventories and pressure the nickel price, Mohr said.
"The longer they stay on strike (lockout), the tighter inventories get. If it lasts long enough, it will have some impact," he said.
Competitor Falconbridge Ltd said the lockout would need to last two more weeks to have an impact.
"Taking Thompson out of the market will definitely mean a deficit," Joe Laezza, vice-president of marketing for Falconbridge, said in a telephone interview.
He said the dispute could easily drag on that long since the two sides seemed so far apart.
The main issues in the dispute are wages and shifts.
Other analysts have estimated it would take four to eight weeks without Thompson production to move the nickel price.
"It takes time for this to happen," Credifinance analyst Tony Hayes said.

Inco has told its customers that supply would not be disrupted because of the labor dispute. The company has said it would use product from its other facilities and if necessary buy nickel from the LME to keep customers supplied.
Inco started to buy extra nickel well in advance of the lockout, industry sources said.
A higher nickel price would boost Inco's profits, but also mean higher costs for the company if it had to turn to the LME to supply its customers.
There was no end in sight on Monday to the labor dispute.
No talks were scheduled, spokesmen for the union and the company said.
Last week, a government conciliator gave up on brokering an agreement because the sides were too far apart. The parties have not met since talks broke down a week ago.
-- Heather Scoffield, Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8104
